full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** I'm downgrading the first pass's KNOWN-VARIANT. What it found new was a particular combination of rules, not a new behaviour, and by your own criterion that doesn't count.

**What the run is doing.** Every feature points to the fragmented, frozen phase of the coevolving voter model. That model has two parts: nodes copy a neighbour's type, and links between different types get rewired. Vazquez, Eguíluz and San Miguel showed it has an absorbing transition from an active to a frozen phase at a critical value p_c = (μ−2)/(μ−1) that depends only on the average degree μ. In finite systems, the active and frozen phases correspond to a connected and a fragmented network respectively. With average degree 4, p_c = 2/3. Your rewiring rate of 1.0 is well above that, so fragmentation is the expected outcome. The general phase picture is also documented: a dynamically active coexistence phase in a single component network, absorbing consensus phase in a single component network, and absorbing phase in a fragmented network. Holme and Newman's earlier model shows the same switch from a regime in which opinions are arbitrarily diverse to one in which most individuals hold the same opinion.

**Why it doesn't look like textbook consensus.** It passes the consensus test because each component agrees internally, not because the whole network agrees. That is what the fragmented phase looks like. The combination of a high component count with a large giant component (n_components ≈ 1.1, n_giant ≈ 0.96) also matches a known pattern. In noisy versions of the model, noise targeting a fraction of nodes preserves the transitions but introduces shattered fragmentation with its characteristic fraction of isolated nodes and one or two giant components. I didn't confirm whether your third rule allows isolated nodes, but the pattern is consistent with that.

**The game layer adds nothing new.** The game step has nodes copy their best-scoring neighbour on an adaptive network with rewiring. That is the Zimmermann–Eguíluz–San Miguel setup: each agent plays a Prisoner's Dilemma game with its local neighbors, collects an aggregate payoff, and imitates the strategy of its best neighbor. Copying the best neighbour combined with network plasticity is also known to drive segregation (the title of a 2023 study of coordination games). Here, if type and strategy are the same thing, the game step is just a second force pushing neighbours to agree. Adding it on top of random-neighbour copying doesn't change which regime the system ends up in.

**Is it genuine or trivial?** The fragmentation is a real emergent effect, but this setup more or less forces it:
- **Edge turnover (0.979)** comes almost directly from the rules: every mixed-type link is cut and rewired on every step.
- **Degree spread (0.625)** is the usual side effect of rewiring to random nodes.
- **Oscillation (0.275)** is moderate. I suspect it comes from updating all nodes at the same time, which lets pairs of neighbours keep swapping types, rather than from any structured cycle. I couldn't find a source on this specifically.
- The two other rule programs in the class (different rule order) behave the same way. That is consistent with the outcome being set by the rewiring rate rather than by how the rules interact.

Nothing in the observed behaviour is left unexplained.
